pages.text: Expect every fight to cost something — mobs here are deliberately tougher than vanilla. That's a core design decision, not a bug: mobs are $(italic)real threats$() that make your class, gear, and skill investments matter.$(br2)$(thing)Base HP multipliers$() apply to all mobs by category before any other scaling.

pages.title: HP Multipliers
pages.text: $(bold)Basic mobs$() (zombies, skeletons, spiders, etc.) — $(thing)3× HP$()$(br)$(bold)Mid-tier mobs$() (endermen, witches, piglins, etc.) — $(thing)1.5× HP$()$(br)$(bold)Bosses$() (Wither, Dragon, mod bosses) — $(thing)Unchanged$()$(br2)Basic mobs get the largest multiplier because they are the most common and should not die in one hit. Bosses are balanced individually and need no blanket scaling.

pages.title: Dimension Stacking
pages.text: HP multipliers $(bold)stack with dimension scaling$(). Each dimension applies its own multiplier on top of the base toughness tier.$(br2)$(bold)Example:$() A zombie (3× base) in the Nether (4× dimension) has $(thing)12×$() its vanilla HP. The same zombie in the End is tougher still.$(br2)Early-dimension mobs in late-game dimensions are not free kills — they scale to stay dangerous.

pages.title: What This Means for You
pages.text: You cannot brute-force IridescentCraft with a stone sword. Invest in your $(thing)class abilities$(), upgrade your $(thing)gear$(), and use $(thing)buffs and enchantments$() to keep pace.$(br2)If a mob feels too tanky, you are probably undergeared for that dimension — rushing one burns repair costs fast.$(br2)$(bold)Next: check $(l:icraft:systems/dimension_mechanics)Dimension Mechanics$(/l) for the expected power level of the zone you're heading into.$()
